2.1: Begin the morning by saying to yourself: today I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, the arrogant, the deceitful, the envious, the unsociable. All these things happen to them because they don't know what is good and what is evil. But I have seen the nature of the good, that it is beautiful, and of the bad, that it is ugly, and the nature of the one who does wrong, that it is akin to me: not only of the same blood or seed, but sharing in the same intelligence and the same portion of the divine. So I cannot be harmed by any of them, for no one can fix on me what is ugly; nor can I be angry with my kinsman, nor hate him. For we are made for cooperation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth. To act against one another, then, is contrary to nature; and it is acting against one another to be irritated and to turn away.
2.2: Whatever this is that I am, it is a little flesh and breath, and the ruling part. Throw away your books; no longer distract yourself: it is not allowed. But as if you were now dying, despise the flesh; it is blood and bones and a network, a web of nerves, veins, and arteries. Look at the breath too, what kind of thing it is: air, and not always the same, but every moment breathed out and drawn in again. The third, then, is the ruling part. Think of it like this: you are an old man; no longer let this part be a slave, no longer be pulled by the strings like a puppet into unsociable movements, no longer be either dissatisfied with your present lot or shrink from the future.
2.3: All that comes from the gods is full of providence. What comes from fortune is not separate from nature, nor without being interwoven and entwined with the things which are ordered by providence. From there all things flow; and besides, there is necessity, and what is for the good of the whole universe, of which you are a part. But whatever the nature of the whole brings, and whatever serves to maintain this nature, is good for every part of nature. Now the universe is preserved, as by the changes of the elements, so by the changes of things made up of the elements. Let these principles be enough for you; let them always be fixed opinions. But throw away the thirst for books, so that you may not die grumbling, but cheerfully, truly, and thankful to the gods from your heart.
2.4: Remember how long you have been putting these things off, and how often you have received an opportunity from the gods, and yet do not use it. You must now at last understand what universe you are a part of, and from what governor of the universe your existence flows, and that a limit of time is fixed for you, which, if you do not use it to clear away the clouds from your mind, will go, and you will go, and it will never return.
2.5: Every moment think steadily, as a Roman and a man, to do what you have in hand with perfect and simple dignity, and with affection, and freedom, and justice, and to give yourself relief from all other thoughts. And you will give yourself relief if you do every act of your life as if it were the last, laying aside all carelessness and passionate turning away from the commands of reason, and all hypocrisy, and self-love, and discontent with the portion that has been given to you. You see how few are the things which, if a man takes hold of them, enable him to live a life that flows in quiet and is like the existence of the gods; for the gods, for their part, will ask nothing more of the one who observes these things.
2.6: Do wrong to yourself, do wrong to yourself, my soul; but you will no longer have the chance to honour yourself. Every man's life is enough. But yours is nearly finished, though your soul does not respect itself, but places your happiness in the souls of others.
2.7: Do the external things that befall you distract you? Give yourself time to learn something new and good, and stop being whirled around. But then you must also avoid being carried about the other way; for those too are triflers who have worn themselves out in life by their activity, and yet have no aim to which to direct every movement and, in a word, all their thoughts.
2.8: A man has seldom been seen to be unhappy through not observing what is in another's mind; but those who do not observe the movements of their own minds must necessarily be unhappy.
2.9: This you must always bear in mind: what the nature of the whole is, and what my nature is, and how this is related to that, and what kind of part it is of what kind of whole; and that there is no one who prevents you from always doing and saying the things which are according to the nature of which you are a part.
2.10: Theophrastus, in his comparison of bad acts—such a comparison as one would make in keeping with the common notions of mankind—says, like a true philosopher, that the offences committed through desire are more blameworthy than those committed through anger. For he who is stirred by anger seems to turn away from reason with a certain pain and unconscious contraction; but he who offends through desire, being overpowered by pleasure, seems in a way to be more intemperate and more womanish in his offences. Rightly, then, and in a way worthy of philosophy, he said that the offence committed with pleasure is more blameworthy than that committed with pain; and on the whole the one is more like a person who has first been wronged and through pain is driven to anger, while the other is moved by his own impulse to do wrong, being carried towards doing something by desire.
2.11: Since it is possible that you may leave life this very moment, regulate every act and thought accordingly. But to go away from among men, if there are gods, is nothing to be afraid of, for the gods will not involve you in evil; but if indeed they do not exist, or if they have no concern for human affairs, what is it to me to live in a universe without gods or without providence? But in truth they do exist, and they do care for human things, and they have put all the means in man's power to enable him not to fall into real evils. And as for the rest, if there were anything evil, they would have provided for this too, that it should be entirely in a man's power not to fall into it. Now, how can that which does not make a man worse make a man's life worse? But it is not possible that the nature of the universe has overlooked these things, either through ignorance, or through having the knowledge but not the power to guard against or correct them; nor is it possible that it has made so great a mistake, through lack of power or lack of skill, that good and evil should happen indiscriminately to the good and the bad. But death certainly, and life, honour and dishonour, pain and pleasure—all these things happen equally to good men and bad, being things which make us neither better nor worse. Therefore they are neither good nor evil.
2.12: How quickly all things disappear—in the universe the bodies themselves, and in time the memory of them. What is the nature of all things perceived by the senses, and especially those which attract with the bait of pleasure, or terrify with pain, or are spread abroad by vaporous fame; how worthless, and contemptible, and sordid, and perishable, and dead they are—all this it is the part of the intellect to observe. To observe too who these are whose opinions and voices give reputation; what death is, and the fact that, if a man looks at it in itself, and by reflection's power of abstraction breaks down into their parts all the things which present themselves to the imagination in it, he will then consider it to be nothing other than an operation of nature; and if anyone is afraid of an operation of nature, he is a child. This, however, is not only an operation of nature, but also a thing which serves the purposes of nature. To observe too how man comes near to the Deity, and by what part of him, and when this part of man is so disposed.
2.13: Nothing is more wretched than a man who goes round everything in a circle, and pries into the things beneath the earth, as the poet says, and tries to guess what is in his neighbours' minds, without seeing that it is enough to attend to the spirit within him, and to revere it sincerely. And reverence for the spirit within consists in keeping it pure from passion and thoughtlessness, and from dissatisfaction with what comes from gods and men. For the things from the gods deserve veneration for their excellence; and the things from men should be dear to us because of kinship; and sometimes even, in a way, they move our pity because of men's ignorance of good and bad—this defect being no less than the one which takes away our power to distinguish things that are white and black.
2.14: Even if you were going to live three thousand years, and as many times ten thousand years, still remember that no man loses any other life than the one he is living now, nor lives any other than the one he is now losing. The longest and the shortest are thus brought to the same. For the present is the same for all, though what passes away is not the same; and so what is lost appears to be a mere moment. For a man cannot lose either the past or the future: for how can anyone take from him what he does not have? These two things, then, you must bear in mind: the first, that all things from eternity are of like forms and come round in a circle, and that it makes no difference whether a man sees the same things for a hundred years, or two hundred, or an infinite time; and the second, that the one who lives longest and the one who will die soonest lose just the same. For the present is the only thing of which a man can be deprived, if it is true that this is the only thing he has, and that a man cannot lose a thing he does not have.
2.15: Remember that all is opinion. For what was said by the Cynic Monimus is clear; and clear too is the use of what was said, if a man takes what can be got out of it as far as it is true.
2.16: The soul of man does violence to itself, first of all, when it becomes an abscess and, as it were, a tumour on the universe, as far as it can. For to be irritated at anything that happens is a separation of ourselves from nature, in some part of which the natures of all other things are contained. Next, the soul does violence to itself when it turns away from any man, or even moves towards him with the intention of harming him, as the souls of those who are angry do. Thirdly, the soul does violence to itself when it is overpowered by pleasure or by pain. Fourthly, when it plays a part, and does or says anything insincerely and untruly. Fifthly, when it allows any act or movement of its own to be without an aim, and does anything thoughtlessly and without considering what it is, since it is right that even the smallest things be done with reference to an end; and the end of rational beings is to follow the reason and the law of the most ancient city and state.
2.17:
Of human life, the time is a point, and the substance is in flux, and perception is dull, and the makeup of the whole body is subject to decay, and the soul is a whirl, and fortune is hard to predict, and fame is a thing without judgement. And, to say it all in a word, everything that belongs to the body is a stream, and what belongs to the soul is a dream and vapour, and life is a war and a stranger's stay in a foreign land, and after fame comes oblivion. What then can guide a man? One thing, and only one: philosophy. And this consists in keeping the spirit within a man free from violence and unharmed, above pains and pleasures, doing nothing without a purpose, nor falsely or with hypocrisy, not needing anyone else to do or not do anything; and besides, accepting all that happens, and all that is allotted, as coming from that same source, wherever it is, from which he himself came; and, finally, waiting for death with a cheerful mind, as nothing other than a dissolving of the elements of which every living being is made. But if there is no harm to the elements themselves in each continually changing into another, why should a man have any fear about the change and dissolution of all the elements? For it is according to nature, and nothing is evil which is according to nature.

Written at Carnuntum.
